title: Testing, Validation, and Root-Cause Analysis
bodyMarkdown:
## Why this matters for the PCA exam

This module covers two halves of the technical-process sub-objective: proving that code and infrastructure behave correctly before and after release, and diagnosing failures fast when they do not. Scenarios describe a cascading failure, a slow release process or a compliance worry, then ask which testing practices and observability tools belong in the process. The strongest answers layer automated tests early, validate infrastructure with policy checks, release progressively, use logs, metrics and traces together, and finish with a blameless postmortem.

## A layered testing strategy

Effort should shift left, because a defect found on a commit costs far less than one found in production.

| Layer | What it checks | Where it runs on Google Cloud |
|---|---|---|
| Unit | Single functions or classes | Cloud Build step on every commit |
| Integration | Components with real or emulated dependencies | Cloud Build with ephemeral dependencies or emulators |
| End-to-end | Complete user journeys | Staging environment mirroring production |
| Performance and load | Throughput and latency at expected and peak load | Load tests against staging |
| Infrastructure | IaC correctness and policy compliance | Terraform plan plus policy check in CI |
| Production validation | Real behavior after release | Cloud Deploy verification, canary, uptime checks |

"Skip staging to save cost when releases are urgent" is a distractor; if cost is the concern, shrink or schedule staging rather than remove it.

### Validating infrastructure, not just code

Infrastructure changes deserve the same pipeline as application changes. Google documents `gcloud beta terraform vet`, which, per the [policy validation guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/terraform/policy-validation/validate-policies), takes the JSON form of a `terraform plan` and validates it against a policy library you maintain. The typical CI sequence is: generate the plan JSON, clone the policy library, run the check, and stop before `terraform apply` on failure. In Google's sample script, exit code 2 means violations were found. Constraints are YAML in a Gatekeeper-style structure. The tool is labeled Pre-GA, "available as is and might have limited support," which matters if a scenario has strict support requirements. Exam wording may call this Policy Validator or OPA-style policy as code; the principle is the same: reject non-compliant changes before they reach any environment.

### Validating releases in production

Production validation complements pre-production tests; it does not replace them.

- **Cloud Deploy verification** runs after deployment and fails the rollout if the verification container exits non-zero, per the [verification documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/verify-deployment). On GKE it can run on the application cluster; on Cloud Run it runs only in the Cloud Deploy execution environment.
- **Canary rollouts** send a portion of traffic to the new version first. Cloud Run, for example, supports a gradual rollout, such as sending 1% of requests to a new revision and increasing the percentage while watching telemetry, per the [Cloud Run overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/overview/what-is-cloud-run).
- **Uptime checks** probe critical endpoints continuously. Per the [uptime checks documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/uptime-checks), the default period is 300 seconds, protocols are HTTP, HTTPS and TCP, and the default alerting condition requires at least two regions to report failures for at least one minute. Public checks reach publicly available targets; private checks cover resources on private networks.
- **Automatic rollback or repair** limits the time a bad release is live; see the Cloud Deploy module for repair automation.

## Root-cause analysis with Google Cloud Observability

Root-cause analysis (RCA) is only as good as your telemetry. The four tools to know, and the question each answers:

| Tool | Question it answers | Facts worth knowing |
|---|---|---|
| Cloud Monitoring | Is something wrong, and since when? | Metrics, dashboards, SLOs, alerting policies, uptime checks |
| Cloud Logging | What did the system say? | Structured logs; Log Analytics runs SQL over log buckets |
| Cloud Trace | Which hop in the request path is slow? | Distributed tracing; 30-day retention in the `_Trace` bucket |
| Error Reporting | Which exceptions are new or growing? | Groups errors by root-cause signature |
| Cloud Profiler | Which function burns CPU or memory? | Continuous production profiling shown as flame graphs |
| Connectivity Tests | Does the network path allow this traffic? | Static analysis of VPC, firewall and routing configuration |

### Cloud Logging and analytics

[Log Analytics](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/log-analytics) lets you run queries that group and aggregate log data, with SQL, to cut troubleshooting time. You upgrade an existing log bucket, and entries written before the upgrade become available once the backfill completes. A linked BigQuery dataset lets you query the same data with BigQuery tools without exporting it, with no BigQuery ingestion or storage cost for the linked dataset, but BigQuery analysis charges apply to the queries you run there. Note that the current docs page presents the capability under the name Observability Analytics; exam wording may still say Log Analytics.

Routing decides where entries go. Per the [routing overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/routing/overview), sinks send entries to log buckets, Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Pub/Sub or another project, each sink has one inclusion filter and optional exclusion filters, and aggregated sinks at the folder or organization level centralize logs. The `_Required` sink cannot be modified. [Retention](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/buckets) is 400 days for `_Required` (not configurable), 30 days for `_Default`, and 1 to 3,650 days for user-defined buckets, with retention beyond the default billed. A bucket's region cannot be changed after creation. [Log-based metrics](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-based-metrics) turn matching entries into counter or distribution metrics for charts and alerts, but only from entries received after the metric is created.

For "who changed what," use [Cloud Audit Logs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit). Admin Activity and System Event logs are always written and cannot be disabled. Data Access logs are disabled by default except for BigQuery and must be enabled explicitly. Admin Activity logs are retained for 400 days in the `_Required` bucket, while the `_Default` bucket holds entries for 30 days. Correlating an incident window with a deploy or configuration change is often the fastest route to the cause.

### Cloud Trace

[Cloud Trace](https://docs.cloud.google.com/trace/docs/overview) tracks request latency across services and shows end-to-end latency, trends over time, and which downstream dependency causes delays, with a heatmap in Trace Explorer. Google recommends OpenTelemetry for instrumentation over the Trace client libraries. Spans in the `_Trace` bucket are kept for 30 days, so a postmortem that waits a month loses the traces.

### Cloud Profiler

[Cloud Profiler](https://docs.cloud.google.com/profiler/docs/about-profiler) is a statistical, low-overhead profiler that continuously collects CPU and memory-allocation data from production and attributes it to source lines, shown as flame graphs. Overhead during collection is under 5 percent and commonly under 0.5 percent amortized, profiles are kept for 30 days, and it supports Go, Java, Node.js and Python. Reach for it when traces show a slow service but not why: Trace finds the slow hop, Profiler finds the hot function inside it. It is not an alerting or sizing tool.

### Error Reporting

[Error Reporting](https://docs.cloud.google.com/error-reporting/docs/grouping-errors) aggregates error events by root cause. Errors with stack traces are grouped by exception type and the five topmost frames; message-only errors are grouped by message and function name, using only the first three literal tokens of the message. A spike in a brand-new group right after a deployment is a strong rollback signal.

### Network diagnosis

When the symptom is "A cannot reach B," start with Network Intelligence Center rather than packet captures. [Connectivity Tests](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/connectivity-tests/concepts/overview) simulates the forwarding path through VPC networks, firewall rules, routes, VPN tunnels and VLAN attachments without sending traffic, and can also run live data-plane probes. Its limits matter: configuration analysis does not model real data-plane behavior, and results take from 30 seconds to 10 minutes. Related [modules](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/overview) include Performance Dashboard (is the network or the app slow?), Firewall Insights and Network Analyzer (misconfigurations). [Gemini Cloud Assist](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cloud-assist/overview) can create AI-driven investigations from logs, errors or a natural-language prompt, but it is a Preview feature whose output must be validated, so it speeds triage rather than replacing the telemetry above.

### Load, chaos and penetration testing

These check behavior that functional tests cannot. Run them against an environment that mirrors production.

- **Load testing:** drive expected and peak traffic, and watch autoscaling and latency SLOs. The Well-Architected [guidance on testing recovery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/reliability/perform-testing-for-recovery-from-failures) adds running load alongside failure scenarios to replicate real usage during an outage.
- **Chaos engineering:** the same guidance suggests simulating failures with tools like Chaos Monkey or custom scripts, escalating scenarios gradually, and repeating periodically, for example quarterly. Define what "normal" looks like first, so you can tell whether the system held. [Fault Injection Testing](https://docs.cloud.google.com/fault-injection-testing/overview) is a Preview service that requires redundancy in the target environment and tightly limited permissions, since its faults cause real disruption.
- **Penetration testing:** per the [Cloud security FAQ](https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/6262505?hl=en), you are not required to notify Google, provided you follow the Acceptable Use Policy and your tests affect only your own projects, not other customers' applications.

## Alerting that supports RCA: SLOs and burn rate

Alert on user-visible symptoms, not every internal metric. An SLO defines the target and the error budget; burn rate measures how fast the budget is being consumed. Per the [burn-rate alerting guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/slo-monitoring/alerting-on-budget-burn-rate), a burn rate above 1 means that if the current error rate persists, the service will violate its SLO. Google Cloud recommends two complementary policies:

| Alert | Threshold | Lookback | Catches |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fast burn | 10x baseline | 1 to 2 hours | Sudden, severe degradation needing immediate response |
| Slow burn | 2x baseline | 24 hours | Sustained over-consumption that would exhaust the budget |

Using both balances speed and noise: short windows react quickly, long windows smooth temporary spikes.

## The RCA loop and blameless postmortems

1. **Detect:** an SLO burn alert or uptime check fires.
2. **Triage:** check dashboards and correlate with recent deploys and audit-log changes.
3. **Diagnose:** move from metrics to logs to traces to isolate the failing component.
4. **Mitigate:** roll back, shift traffic or fail over first; root cause comes second when users are affected.
5. **Learn:** write a postmortem and turn each finding into an automated test, alert or runbook.

Google SRE's [postmortem culture chapter](https://sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/) states that a postmortem "is not punishment" but a learning opportunity, and that blameless postmortems assume everyone "had good intentions and did the right thing with the information they had." You cannot fix people, but you can fix systems and processes. It also advises defining postmortem criteria before incidents occur, for example user-visible degradation beyond a threshold, any data loss, on-call interventions such as a rollback or traffic reroute, long resolution time, or monitoring failures that required manual discovery. And "an unreviewed postmortem might as well never have existed."

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **Blame-oriented reviews.** They teach people to hide incidents. The fix is systemic: missing test, missing alert, unsafe default.
- **Only testing in production.** Relying on users to report defects is never correct.
- **Alerting on causes instead of symptoms.** CPU alerts without SLO alerts create noise and still miss real customer impact.
- **Policy checks after apply.** Validate the plan before `apply`; detecting drift afterwards is too late for preventive guardrails.
- **Debugging before mitigating.** If a deploy caused the incident, roll back first and investigate after.
- **Chaos testing without redundancy or guardrails.** Injecting faults into a system with no replicas, or granting the permission broadly, just creates an outage.
- **Ignoring retention.** Trace spans live 30 days and `_Default` log entries 30 days; export or extend retention if postmortems or audits may need older data.

## Exam tips

- **Correlating logs, metrics and traces:** the answer is Cloud Logging, Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Trace together. Cloud Build triggers, Artifact Registry scanning and Cloud Deploy approvals are distractors for RCA.
- **Testing strategy answers are layered:** unit and integration tests in Cloud Build on every commit, Terraform plan validated with policy checks before apply, and canary with verification for release.
- **Never pick** "deploy straight to production and rely on user reports" or "skip staging to save cost."
- **Fast and slow burn:** the documented pair is 10x with a 1 to 2 hour lookback and 2x with a 24 hour lookback.
- **Blameless means systemic.** Look for options that focus on process fixes and action items, not on disciplining an engineer.
- **Mitigate first.** In an active incident, rolling back or failing over precedes deep diagnosis.
- **Audit logs answer "who changed what."** Admin Activity is always on; Data Access is off by default except BigQuery.
- **Profiler versus Trace:** Trace finds the slow service hop; Cloud Profiler finds the hot function (CPU or memory) with under 5 percent overhead. Connectivity Tests answers "can A reach B" by analyzing configuration, not by sending traffic.
- **Chaos and penetration tests:** escalate failures gradually, run load alongside them, and repeat periodically; no notice to Google is required for penetration tests of your own projects.
- **Trace retention is 30 days** and OpenTelemetry is the recommended instrumentation.
